items.question: How do you see Marble’s usefulness today fitting into your longer-term vision of spatial intelligence?
items.object: Marble’s role as a product and a world model
items.answer: So Marble, basically, one way of looking at it, it's the system. It's a generative model of 3D worlds, right? So you can input things like text or image or multiple images, and it will generate for you a 3D world that kind of matches those inputs. So while Marble is simultaneously a world model that is building towards this vision of spatial intelligence, it was also very intentionally designed to be a thing that people could find useful today. And we're starting to see emerging use cases in gaming, in VFX, in film, where I think there's a lot of really interesting stuff that Marble can do today as a product and then also set a foundation for the grand world models that we want to build going into the future.

items.question: How did your experience of the ImageNet era shape your sense of where computer vision should go next?
items.object: The direction of computer vision after the ImageNet era
items.answer: After that, seeing that ImageNet era during my PhD, I had the sense that the next decade of computer vision was going to be about getting AI out of the data center and out into the world. So a lot of my interests post-PhD shifted into 3D vision, a little bit more into computer graphics, more into generative modeling. I thought I was drifting away from my adviser post-PhD, but when we reunited a couple years later, it turned out she was thinking of very similar things.

items.question: How do you see the growth in available compute creating an opportunity for world models?
items.object: Compute scaling and the opportunity for world models
items.answer: I think one is just there is a lot more data and compute generally available. I think the whole history of deep learning is in some sense the history of scaling up compute. AlexNet required this jump from CPUs to GPUs, but even from AlexNet to today we're getting about a thousand times more performance per card than we had in AlexNet days. Now it's common to train models not just on one GPU but on hundreds or thousands or tens of thousands or even more. So the amount of compute that we can marshal today on a single model is about a millionfold more than we could have even at the start of my PhD. Language was one of the really interesting things that started to work quite well the last couple of years. But as we think about moving towards visual data and spatial data and world data, you just need to process a lot more. I think that's going to be a good way to soak up this new compute that's coming online more and more.

items.object: The choice between industry and academia in computer vision research
items.answer: I had done some computer vision even as an undergrad, and I thought it was really cool and wanted to keep doing it. So then I was sort of faced with this industry-academia choice, even coming out of undergrad, that I think a lot of people in the research community are facing now.

items.question: What drew you to working on LSTMs and RNN language models in 2015?
items.object: LSTMs and RNN language modeling in 2015
items.answer: I remember the group meeting where Andre was presenting some of those results and explaining this new thing called LSTMs and RNNs that I had never heard of before, and I thought, “Wow, this is really amazing stuff. I want to work on that.” So then he had the paper at CVPR 2015 on the first image-captioning results. After that we started working together and first did a paper just on language modeling, back in 2015. I should have stuck with language modeling; that turned out to be pretty lucrative in retrospect. We did this language-modeling paper together, me and Andre, in 2015, where we trained these little RNN language models that could spit out a couple sentences at a time, and we could poke at them and try to understand what the neurons inside the neural network were doing.

items.question: What did you find compelling about looking inside LSTM language models to understand how they processed code?
items.object: Empirical analysis of internal LSTM behavior in language models
items.answer: It was really cool. Even at that time we had results where you could look inside the LSTM and say, “Oh, this thing is reading code.” One of the datasets we trained on was the Linux source code, because the whole thing is open source and you could just download it. We trained an RNN on this dataset and then, as the network was trying to predict the tokens, tried to correlate the kinds of predictions it was making with the internal structures in the RNN. We found some correlations: this unit in this layer of the LSTM fires when there's an open parenthesis and turns off when there's a closed parenthesis. We tried some empirical stuff like that to figure it out. That was pretty cool, and that was sort of cutting out the CNN from this language-modeling part and just looking at the language models in isolation.

items.question: What made the dense-captioning system you built for CVPR 2016 a particularly complicated neural network in your view?
items.object: The architecture of the CVPR 2016 dense-captioning system
items.answer: We built this system that did dense captioning. You input a single image and it would draw boxes around all the interesting stuff in the image and write a short snippet about each of them: “It's a green water bottle on the table. It's a person wearing a black shirt.” This was a really complicated neural network, built on a lot of advancements that had been made in object detection around that time, which was a major topic in computer vision for a long time. It was one joint neural network that was learning to look at individual images. It had three different representations inside the network. One was the representation of the whole image to get the gestalt of what's going on. Then it would propose individual regions it wanted to focus on and represent each region independently. Once you look at the region, you need to spit out text for each region. So that was a pretty complicated neural network architecture. This was all pre-PyTorch.

items.question: What impressed you about showing your real-time captioning demo at ICCV 2015 in Santiago?
items.object: Real-time captioning demo at ICCV 2015 in Santiago
items.answer: We had a conference that year in Santiago, ICCV 15. I had a paper at that conference for something different, but I had my laptop. I was walking around the conference with my laptop showing everybody this real-time captioning demo, and the model was running on a server in California. It was actually able to stream all the way from California down to Santiago. The latency was terrible. It was like 1 FPS, but the fact that it worked at all was pretty amazing.

items.question: How do you weigh pixels against the tokenized text representations used in LLMs?
items.object: Pixels versus tokenized text as representations
items.answer: I think you actually lose something if you translate to these purely tokenized representations that we use in LLMs, right? You lose the font, you lose the line breaks, you lose the 2D arrangement on the page. For a lot of cases, maybe that doesn't matter. But for some things it does. I think pixels are this more lossless representation of what's going on in the world and, in some ways, a more general representation that better matches what we humans see as we navigate the world. So there's an efficiency argument to be made: maybe it's not super efficient to render your text to an image and then feed that to a vision model.

items.question: How do you think about teaching 3D world models the underlying physics in their data?
items.object: Explicit versus latent learning of physics in 3D world models
items.answer: I think there are different ways you could approach that problem. One is you could try to be explicit about it and say, “I want to measure all the forces and feed those as training data to your model.” You could run a traditional physics simulation, know all the forces in the scene, and use those as training data to train a model that's hopefully going to predict those. Or you could hope that something emerges more latently: you train on something end to end, on a more general problem, and hope that something in the internals of the model must learn to model something like physics in order to make the proper predictions. Those are the two big paradigms that we have more generally.

The paper you mentioned is that problem: it learns to fit the specific patterns of orbits, but then it doesn't actually generalize in the way you'd like. It doesn't have a causal model of gravity.

items.question: How do you think about whether AI models understand things compared with how humans understand things?
items.object: Understanding in AI models versus human intelligence
items.answer: There's this trick with understanding. These models are a very different kind of intelligence than human intelligence. Human intelligence is interesting because I think I understand things because I can introspect my own thought process to some extent. Then I believe that my thought process probably works similarly to other people's, so that when I observe someone else's behavior, I infer that their internal mental state is probably similar to my own internal mental state that I've observed. Therefore, I know that I understand things. So I assume that you understand something. But these models are this alien form of intelligence where they can do really interesting things and exhibit really interesting behavior. Whatever kind of internal cognition or self-reflection they have, if it exists at all, is totally different from what we do.

items.question: How do you think about the prospect of one model handling both visual generation and physically reliable architectural design?
items.object: Emergent physical understanding in a unified visual and architectural generation model
items.answer: Yeah, I would like it to be one model, but I think the big problem in deep learning in some sense is: how do you get emergent capabilities beyond your training data? Are you going to get something that understands the forces while it wasn't trained to predict the forces, but it's going to learn them implicitly internally? A lot of what we've seen in other large models is that a lot of this emergent behavior does happen at scale. Will that transfer to other modalities, other use cases, and other tasks? I hope so, but that'll be a process that we need to play out over time and see.

items.question: How did you approach balancing Marble’s long-term spatial intelligence ambitions with making it useful to people today?
items.object: Marble’s balance between spatial intelligence research and a useful product
items.answer: With Marble, we were actually trying to do two things simultaneously, and I think we managed to pull off the balance pretty well. One is build a model that goes towards the grand vision of spatial intelligence. Models need to be able to understand lots of different kinds of inputs, model worlds in a lot of situations, and model counterfactuals of how they could change over time. We wanted to start to build models that have these capabilities, and Marble today does already have hints of all of these. But at the same time, we're a company. We're a business. We were really trying not to have this be a science project, but also build a product that would be useful to people in the real world today. items.question: How do you think about the difference in camera control between Marble and video generative models?
items.object: Camera control in Marble compared with video generative models
items.answer: I find when I play with video generative models, I'm having to learn the language of being a director, because I have to move them, pan, you know? You cannot say “pan 63 degrees to the north,” right? You just don't have that control. Whereas in Marble, you have precise control in terms of placing your camera. I think that's one of the first things people need to understand: you're not generating frame by frame, which is what a lot of the other models are.

items.question: How do you think about the fundamental building blocks of World Labs’ generated 3D worlds?
items.object: The atomic units of World Labs’ world models
items.answer: I think there's what exists today and what could exist in the future. What exists today is the model natively outputs splats. Gaussian splats are tiny particles; each one is semi-transparent and has a position and orientation in 3D space. The scene is built up from a large number of these Gaussian splats. Gaussian splats are really cool because you can render them in real time really efficiently. You can render on your iPhone. That's how we get precise camera control, because the splats can be rendered in real time on pretty much any client-side device that we want. For a lot of the scenes we're generating today, that kind of atomic unit is the individual splat, but I don't think that's fundamental. I could imagine other approaches in the future that would be interesting. There are other approaches that even we've worked on at World Labs, like our recent RTFM model that does generate frames one at a time. There the atomic unit is generating frames one at a time as the user interacts with the system. Or you could imagine other architectures where the atomic unit is a token, where that token represents some chunk of the 3D world. I think there are a lot of different architectures we can experiment with over time.

items.question: How do you think about the tradeoffs between different approaches to adding physics and interaction to 3D scenes represented by Gaussian splats?
items.object: Adding physics, dynamics, and interaction to 3D scenes represented by Gaussian splats
items.answer: Gaussian splats are themselves little particles. There have been a lot of approaches where you attach physical properties to those splats and say that each one has a mass, or maybe treat each one as being coupled with some kind of virtual spring to nearby neighbors. Now you can start to do physics simulation on top of splats. One avenue for adding physics, dynamics, or interaction to these things would be to predict physical properties associated with each splat particle and then simulate those downstream, either using classical physics or something learned. The beauty of working in 3D is things compose, and you can inject logic in different places. One way is to generate a 3D scene, predict 3D properties of everything in the scene, then use a classical physics engine to simulate the interaction. Or you could do something where, as a result of a user action, the model regenerates the entire scene in splats or some other representation. That could potentially be a lot more general because then you're not bound to whatever physical properties you know how to model already. But that's also a lot more computationally demanding because you need to regenerate the whole scene in response to user actions. I think this is a really interesting area for future work and for adding on to potential Marble 2.

items.question: How do you think about the constraints on achieving higher resolution in Gaussian splat scenes?
items.object: Gaussian splat scene resolution and rendering constraints
items.answer: One of the big constraints that we have on our scenes is we wanted things to render cleanly on mobile and in VR headsets. Those devices have a lot less compute than you're used to having in other situations. If you want to get a splat file to render at high resolution, at 30 to 60 FPS on an iPhone from four years ago, then you are a bit limited in the number of splats you can handle. But if you're allowed to work on a recent iPhone or a recent MacBook, or if you have a local GPU, or if you don't need 60 FPS at 1080p, then you can relax the constraints and get away with more splats, and that lets you get higher resolution in your scenes.

items.question: How do you see the scope of applications for the technology powering Marble?
items.object: The technology powering Marble and its potential applications
items.answer: We always view this as a pretty horizontal technology that should be able to touch a lot of different industries over time. Marble is a little bit more focused on creative industries for now, but I think the technology that powers it should be applicable to a lot of different things over time. Robotics is one that is maybe going to happen sooner than later.
quotes: We always view this as a pretty horizontal technology that should be able to touch a lot of different industries over time. Marble is a little bit more focused on creative industries for now, but I think the technology that powers it should be applicable to a lot of different things over time. Robotics is one that is maybe going to happen sooner than later.

rubrics.text: The response distinguishes Marble’s current creative-industry focus from the broader cross-industry scope of its underlying technology.
The response identifies robotics as a potentially near-term application of the technology powering Marble.

items.question: How do you see Marble's usefulness for kitchen remodeling in relation to its broader capabilities?
items.object: Marble's emergent uses for kitchen remodeling and interior design
items.answer: I was joking online. I posted this video on Slack: “Who wants to use Marble to plan your next kitchen remodel?” It actually works great for this already. Take two images of your kitchen, reconstruct it in Marble, and then use the editing features to see what that space would look like if you changed the countertops, floors, or cabinets. This isn't something we necessarily built specifically for this use case, but because it's a powerful horizontal technology, you get these emergent use cases that fall out of the model. We have early beta users using an API key that's already building for interior design use cases.

items.question: How do you frame the open questions around spatial intelligence in relation to LLMs?
items.object: Spatial intelligence in relation to LLM intelligence
items.answer: I'm curious about the whole spatial intelligence space. I think we should dig more into that one. How do you define it, and what are the gaps between traditional intelligence that people might think about with LLMs—when Dario says we have a data center full of Einstein, that's traditional intelligence, it's not spatial intelligence—what is required to be spatially intelligent?
quotes: I'm curious about the whole spatial intelligence space. I think we should dig more into that one. How do you define it, and what are the gaps between traditional intelligence that people might think about with LLMs—when Dario says we have a data center full of Einstein, that's traditional intelligence, it's not spatial intelligence—what is required to be spatially intelligent?

rubrics.text: The response distinguishes the intelligence represented by Dario’s “data center full of Einsteins” from spatial intelligence.

items.question: How do you think about the ways spatial and linguistic intelligence can help each other?
items.object: The interplay of spatial and linguistic intelligence
items.answer: If I think about Sir Isaac Newton, you have things like gravity that at the time had not been formalized in language, that people inherently spatially understand: things fall. But then it's helpful to formalize that in some way, or all these different rules we use language to capture something that empirically and spatially you can also understand, but it's easier to describe in a way. I'm curious about the interplay of spatial and linguistic intelligence. Some rules are easier to write in language for spatial intelligence to understand, but you cannot write, “Put your hand like this and put it down this amount.” I'm always curious about how they leverage each other together.

rubrics.text: The response states that language can formalize rules that people already understand intuitively through spatial experience.
The response states that some spatial actions cannot be fully specified through verbal instructions.

items.question: How do you understand spatial intelligence in relation to the abstract reasoning of large language models?
items.object: Spatial intelligence and its relationship to language-based reasoning
items.answer: It's useful to distinguish between theory building versus the embodied daily experience of being embedded in the three-dimensional world. To me, spatial intelligence encapsulates that embodied experience of being there in 3D space, moving through it, seeing it, actioning it. As Fei-Fei said, you can narrate those things, but it's a very lossy channel. The notion of being in the world and doing things in it is a very different modality from trying to describe it. But because we as humans are animals who have evolved interacting in space all the time, we don't even think that's a hard thing. We naturally leap to language and then theory building as mechanisms to abstract above that native spatial understanding. In some sense, LLMs have jumped all the way to those highest forms of abstracted reasoning, which is very interesting and useful. But spatial intelligence is almost like opening up that black box again and saying maybe we've lost something by going straight to that fully abstracted form of language and reasoning and communication.

items.question: Why do you think a model of the world based entirely on word sequences struggles to rule out physical impossibilities?
items.object: Word-sequence models of the world and physical impossibility
items.answer: And that's what I mean about unwrapping this abstraction. If your whole model of the world is just saying sequences of words after each other, it's really hard to say, “Why not?”
quotes: And that's what I mean about unwrapping this abstraction. If your whole model of the world is just saying sequences of words after each other, it's really hard to say, “Why not?”

items.question: How do you think about giving language models the spatial intelligence that makes physical impossibilities obvious to humans?
items.object: Spatial intelligence in language models
items.answer: The reason it's obvious to us is because we're internally mapping it back to some three-dimensional representation of the world that we're familiar with. The question is, how hard is it, how long is it going to take us to distill from— I use the word distill; I don't know if you agree with that—to distill from your world models into a language model? We do want our models to have spatial intelligence, right? Do we have to throw language models out completely in order to do that, or—
quotes: But the reason it's obvious to us is because we're internally mapping it back to some three-dimensional representation of the world that we're familiar with.

items.question: Why do you expect language interfaces to remain useful even if AI develops a universal model?
items.object: Language interfaces for AI systems
items.answer: There's a pragmatic thing where people use language and want to interact with systems using language. Even pragmatically, it's useful to build systems, products, and models that let people talk to them. I don't see that going away.
quotes: there's a pragmatic thing where people use language and want to interact with systems using language. Even pragmatically, it's useful to build systems, products, and models that let people talk to them. I don't see that going away.

rubrics.text: The response attributes the continued usefulness of language interfaces to people's preference for interacting with systems through language.

items.question: What interests you intellectually about building a model that uses only vision or spatial intelligence?
items.object: Models that use only vision or spatial intelligence
items.answer: I think there's an intellectual curiosity of saying, intellectually, how much could you build a model that only uses vision or only uses spatial intelligence? I don't know that that would be practically useful, but it would be an interesting intellectual or academic exercise to see how far you could push that. Not to bring it back to physics, but I'm curious: if you had a highly precise world model and didn't give it any notion of our current understanding of the standard model of physics, how much of it would be able to come up with and recreate from scratch, and what level of language understanding would it need? We have so many notations that we create, but maybe we'll come up with a very different model of it and still be accurate. I wonder how much we're limited. People say humans need to be like humans because the world is built for humans, and in a way the way we build language constrains some of the outputs we can get from these other modalities as well.

items.question: How do you decide which existing AI architectures to keep when working on new modalities?
items.object: Retaining existing AI architectures when working on new modalities
items.answer: I think you stick with stuff that works. Attention is still there. You don't need to fix things that aren't broken. There's a lot of hard problems in the world to solve, but let's focus on one at a time. I think it is interesting to think about new architectures or new paradigms or drastically different ways to learn, but you don't need to throw away everything just because you're working on new modalities.
quotes: I think you stick with stuff that works. Attention is still there. You don't need to fix things that aren't broken. There's a lot of hard problems in the world to solve, but let's focus on one at a time. I think it is interesting to think about new architectures or new paradigms or drastically different ways to learn, but you don't need to throw away everything just because you're working on new modalities.

rubrics.text: The response states that working on a new modality does not by itself justify discarding architectures that already work.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between transformers and sequence modeling?
items.object: Transformers as models of sets rather than sequences
items.answer: I think there's a little bit of technological confusion. Transformers already solved that for us, right? Transformers are actually not a model of sequences. A transformer is natively a model of sets. That's very powerful, but because a lot of the transformers grew out of earlier architectures based around recurrent neural networks, and RNNs definitely do have built into their architecture that they model one-dimensional sequences—

rubrics.text: The response states that transformers natively model sets.

items.question: Why do you view a transformer as a model of a set of tokens rather than a sequence?
items.object: Transformers as architectures for sets of tokens
items.answer: A transformer is actually not a model of a sequence of tokens. A transformer is a model of a set of tokens. The only thing that injects the order into the standard transformer architecture—the only thing that differentiates the order of the things—is the positional embedding you give the tokens. If you choose to give it a 1D positional embedding, that's the only mechanism the model has to know that it's a 1D sequence. All the operators that happen inside a transformer block are either token-wise—you have an FFN, QKV projections, per-token normalization, all of those happen independently per token—or you have interactions between tokens through the attention mechanism. That's permutation equivariant, so if I permute my tokens, then the attention operator gets a permuted output in exactly the same way. So it's natively an architecture of sets of tokens.
